title: Clarithromycin and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Drink on Biaxin?
excerpt: Can you drink on clarithromycin? How it interacts with alcohol and other drugs, why H. pylori treatment changes the answer, how long to wait, and warning signs.
metaDescription: Can you drink on clarithromycin? How it interacts with alcohol, why H. pylori treatment changes the answer, how long to wait, and warning signs.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** clarithromycin does not set off the severe flushing and vomiting reaction that a few antibiotics cause with alcohol, and the UK's NHS guidance says you can drink while taking it. That doesn't make it a free pass. Clarithromycin is one of the most interaction-prone antibiotics there is, because it blocks a liver enzyme that clears dozens of other drugs. It can also affect your heart rhythm, and it often upsets the stomach on its own. For most healthy adults, a drink or two is unlikely to cause harm. Heavy drinking is a bad idea, and if your clarithromycin is part of an H. pylori kit that includes metronidazole, you should avoid alcohol completely.

**The quick rules:** Ask your prescriber or pharmacist before drinking, especially if you take other medicines. If they say it's fine, keep it light and drink with food. Skip alcohol entirely if you're being treated for H. pylori or a stomach ulcer, especially if metronidazole is in the mix. Be extra careful if you take sleeping pills, anxiety medicine, opioid painkillers, or diabetes medicine, because clarithromycin can make some of those much stronger, and alcohol adds to the effect. Never skip or delay a dose because you've been drinking.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and full medication list. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking on clarithromycin if** you have heart disease, a known long QT interval, liver or kidney disease, diabetes treated with insulin or sulfonylureas, or you take any sedating medicine, statin, blood thinner, or heart rhythm drug. **Get medical help right away** if you have fainting, a racing or irregular heartbeat, chest pain, severe or bloody diarrhea, yellow skin or eyes, or signs of an allergic reaction such as swelling of the face or trouble breathing. In an emergency, call 911.

## How Clarithromycin and Alcohol Actually Interact

Clarithromycin is a **macrolide** antibiotic, the same family as azithromycin (the Z-Pak) and erythromycin. It stops bacteria from making the proteins they need to grow. It's commonly prescribed for chest infections and pneumonia, sinus infections, strep throat in people allergic to penicillin, some skin infections, and as part of combination treatment for **H. pylori**, the stomach bacterium behind many ulcers.

To understand the alcohol question, it helps to separate what clarithromycin does to alcohol from what it does to everything else.

### What it doesn't do: no disulfiram-like reaction

Some antibiotics, most famously metronidazole and tinidazole, are linked to a reaction with alcohol that resembles the effect of disulfiram, a drug used to make drinking unpleasant. The reaction can include flushing, a pounding heart, nausea, and vomiting. Clarithromycin is not one of those drugs. It doesn't block the enzyme that clears acetaldehyde, the toxic by-product of alcohol, so a drink won't make you suddenly sick in that way.

Clarithromycin also has little effect on how fast your body clears alcohol. Your liver breaks down alcohol mainly with an enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase, plus a backup enzyme called CYP2E1. Clarithromycin works on a different enzyme, so your blood alcohol level after a drink should be about what it normally would be.

### What it does do: it blocks CYP3A4

Here's the part that matters. Clarithromycin is a **strong inhibitor of CYP3A4**, a liver and gut enzyme that breaks down a huge number of common medicines. When CYP3A4 is blocked, those medicines build up in your blood to higher levels than your doctor intended.

Clarithromycin also blocks this enzyme in a lasting way. Rather than just getting in the way while it's present, it disables the enzyme molecules it binds to, and your body has to make fresh ones. That's why its interaction effects can linger for a few days after the last pill.

Alcohol enters the picture as a multiplier. If clarithromycin has pushed up the level of a sedating drug, such as certain sleeping pills, anxiety medicines, or opioid painkillers, alcohol stacks its own sedation on top. The combination can cause much more drowsiness, slowed breathing, poor coordination, and dangerous falls than either would alone.

### It can affect heart rhythm

Clarithromycin can lengthen the **QT interval**, the stretch of time the heart's lower chambers take to recharge between beats. In rare cases a long QT can trigger a dangerous irregular rhythm. In 2018 the FDA also issued a safety communication advising doctors to weigh the risks carefully before prescribing clarithromycin to people with heart disease, after a long-term follow-up study found more deaths in heart patients who had taken it.

Alcohol doesn't directly cause that problem, but heavy drinking can make it more likely. A binge can cause vomiting and fluid loss, which drain potassium and magnesium, and low levels of both make the heart more prone to rhythm problems. Heavy drinking also triggers rhythm disturbances on its own in some people, a pattern doctors sometimes call "holiday heart." For a healthy person having a drink or two, this is a remote concern. For someone with heart disease or on other QT-prolonging medicines, it's a reason to avoid drinking during the course.

### The side effects overlap

Clarithromycin's most common side effects are nausea, diarrhea, stomach pain, a bitter or metallic taste, and headache. Those are also classic hangover symptoms. Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and speeds up the gut, so drinking can make the antibiotic's stomach effects noticeably worse. It also makes it harder to tell whether you feel bad from the drug, the drinks, or the infection itself.

## Is It Safe to Drink on Clarithromycin? What the Guidance Says

Official guidance is fairly consistent:

- **The UK's NHS** says you can drink alcohol while taking clarithromycin.
- **The US prescribing information** for clarithromycin does not list alcohol as a contraindication. Its long warnings focus instead on drug interactions, heart rhythm (QT prolongation), liver problems, and severe diarrhea caused by *C. difficile*.
- **Pharmacists commonly advise moderation** with any antibiotic. Your body is fighting an infection, and alcohol can disrupt sleep, add to dehydration, and make side effects harder to tolerate.

So "can you drink" has a reasonable answer: a small amount is generally acceptable for a healthy person who isn't on interacting medicines. "Should you drink" is a separate question. If you're sick enough to need antibiotics, a few days off usually costs you very little and helps you recover.

## The Interactions That Actually Matter

This is where clarithromycin and alcohol become a real safety issue. The table below lists common drug types that clarithromycin can boost, and why alcohol makes each combination riskier. It's not a complete list, and your pharmacist can check your exact medicines.

| If you also take... | What clarithromycin does | Why alcohol adds risk |
|---|---|---|
| Certain sleeping pills and anxiety medicines (for example triazolam, midazolam, alprazolam) | Can raise their levels substantially | Much stronger sedation, slowed breathing, falls |
| Opioid painkillers (for example oxycodone, fentanyl) | Can raise their levels | Extra sedation and breathing suppression, which can be dangerous |
| Some statins (simvastatin and lovastatin are contraindicated) | Raises levels sharply, raising the risk of serious muscle damage | Heavy drinking also strains muscles and the liver |
| Diabetes medicines (insulin, sulfonylureas like glipizide or glyburide) | Low blood sugar has been reported with the combination | Alcohol can also drop blood sugar, especially without food |
| Colchicine (for gout) | Can raise levels to toxic, sometimes fatal, amounts | Adds stomach upset and dehydration |
| Some blood pressure and heart drugs (certain calcium channel blockers) | Can raise levels, causing low blood pressure | Alcohol lowers blood pressure too, causing dizziness or fainting |
| Warfarin | Can increase its effect and bleeding risk | Heavy drinking also changes how warfarin works |
| Erectile dysfunction drugs (sildenafil, tadalafil) | Raises their levels | Both lower blood pressure, raising the risk of dizziness and fainting |

A few practical points:

- **Tell the prescriber everything you take**, including over-the-counter sleep aids and supplements. Clarithromycin is often prescribed quickly for a chest or sinus infection, and interactions get missed.
- **If you take any sedating medicine, the safest choice is no alcohol** for the whole course and a few days after.
- **If you're on a statin**, your doctor may tell you to pause it while you take clarithromycin. Follow that advice. Our guide to [statins and alcohol](/never-hungover/statins-and-alcohol) covers the drinking side of statins on their own.

## Clarithromycin, Alcohol, and H. Pylori Treatment

A large share of clarithromycin prescriptions are for H. pylori. If that's you, the alcohol answer changes.

H. pylori is usually treated with several drugs at once: an acid reducer (a proton pump inhibitor such as omeprazole, or the newer drug vonoprazan) plus two or more antibiotics. Common combinations that include clarithromycin are:

- **Triple therapy:** acid reducer + clarithromycin + amoxicillin, or acid reducer + clarithromycin + metronidazole.
- **Concomitant therapy:** acid reducer + clarithromycin + amoxicillin + metronidazole, all taken together.
- **Packaged kits:** some prescriptions come as blister packs containing all the drugs for each day.

Recent US treatment guidelines have moved away from using clarithromycin-based triple therapy unless testing shows the bacteria are still sensitive to it, because resistance has grown. You may get a different regimen, but clarithromycin is still widely used.

**Why to skip alcohol during H. pylori treatment:**

1. **Metronidazole is often in the mix.** Drinking while taking metronidazole can cause flushing, a racing heart, nausea, and vomiting. Its label advises avoiding alcohol during treatment and for at least three days after the last dose. If you're not sure whether your kit includes it, read the label or ask the pharmacist. Our [metronidazole and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/metronidazole-and-alcohol) explains the 72-hour rule, and if it's already happened, see [what to do if you accidentally drank on metronidazole](/never-hungover/accidentally-drank-on-metronidazole).
2. **Alcohol irritates an inflamed stomach.** If you have an ulcer or gastritis, alcohol can worsen pain and slow healing while the treatment is trying to fix the problem.
3. **Side effects pile up.** Taking three or four drugs together already causes a lot of nausea, diarrhea, and bad taste. Alcohol makes it harder to stick with the regimen, and finishing every dose is one of the biggest factors in whether H. pylori treatment works.

H. pylori courses usually last 10 to 14 days. Two weeks without alcohol is a reasonable price for clearing an infection that can cause recurring ulcers.

## Does Alcohol Make Clarithromycin Less Effective?

There is no good evidence that a moderate amount of alcohol stops clarithromycin from killing bacteria. Alcohol doesn't meaningfully change how the drug is absorbed or how fast it's cleared.

The real risks to effectiveness are practical ones:

- **Vomiting a dose.** If you throw up soon after taking a pill, some of the dose may be lost. Call your pharmacist for advice rather than guessing whether to take another.
- **Missed or late doses.** Clarithromycin is often taken every 12 hours. A late night makes it easy to sleep through the morning dose.
- **Slower recovery.** Heavy drinking disrupts sleep, dehydrates you, and can dampen your immune response, which can leave you feeling sick for longer even when the antibiotic is doing its job.

For more on this question across all antibiotic types, see our guide on whether [alcohol makes antibiotics less effective](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-make-antibiotics-less-effective).

## How Long After Clarithromycin Can You Drink?

There's no official waiting period for clarithromycin on its own. Here's how to think about it:

- **The drug itself clears fairly quickly.** Clarithromycin's half-life (the time it takes for the level in your blood to drop by half) is several hours, so most of it is gone within about a day of your last dose. Its active by-product lasts somewhat longer.
- **The enzyme effect lasts longer.** Because clarithromycin disables CYP3A4 rather than just blocking it temporarily, interactions with other medicines can last a few days after you stop. If you take a sedating drug or another interacting medicine, waiting two to three days before drinking is a sensible cushion.
- **If metronidazole was part of your treatment,** wait at least 72 hours after your last metronidazole dose.
- **If you're still sick,** give yourself a day or two of recovery anyway. Finishing the pills doesn't mean the infection has fully settled.

Our guide on [how long to wait after antibiotics before drinking](/never-hungover/how-long-after-antibiotics-can-you-drink) compares waiting times across the most common antibiotics.

## Clarithromycin vs Other Antibiotics With Alcohol

People often compare clarithromycin to other antibiotics they've taken. Here's how it stacks up:

| Antibiotic | Severe reaction with alcohol? | Main caution |
|---|---|---|
| Clarithromycin | No | Many drug interactions (CYP3A4), heart rhythm, stomach upset |
| Azithromycin (Z-Pak) | No | Stomach upset, rare heart rhythm effects, fewer drug interactions than clarithromycin |
| Amoxicillin | No | Mostly stomach upset; few interactions |
| Metronidazole | Yes, historically linked | Avoid alcohol during and for 72 hours after |
| Tinidazole | Yes, historically linked | Label advises avoiding alcohol during and for 3 days after |

If you've been fine drinking on a Z-Pak before, don't assume clarithromycin is identical. They're in the same family, but clarithromycin has many more drug interactions. Our [azithromycin and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/azithromycin-and-alcohol) and [amoxicillin and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/amoxicillin-and-alcohol) cover those two in detail, and the [antibiotics and alcohol overview](/never-hungover/antibiotics-and-alcohol) covers the rest.

## Clarithromycin With Beer, Wine, or Liquor

The type of drink doesn't change the interaction. What matters is the total amount of alcohol. A standard drink in the US is roughly a 12-ounce beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, or a 1.5-ounce shot of spirits.

A few practical notes for social drinkers:

- **Keep it light**, within whatever limit your prescriber or pharmacist gives you, and space drinks out.
- **Drink with a meal.** Food helps buffer the stomach, and the extended-release tablet should be taken with food anyway.
- **Alternate with water.** Clarithromycin can cause diarrhea, and alcohol adds to fluid loss.
- **Expect a worse morning.** Between the drug's bitter taste, nausea, and diarrhea, a hangover on clarithromycin often feels rougher than usual.
- **Don't drink on the same night as a sleep aid**, even an over-the-counter one, while you're on clarithromycin.

## If You've Already Been Drinking on Clarithromycin

If you had a few drinks and feel more or less normal, you don't need to panic. Take your next dose on schedule, drink water, eat something, and skip more alcohol for the rest of the course.

**Get medical help right away if you notice:**

- Fainting, near-fainting, or a racing, fluttering, or irregular heartbeat
- Chest pain or shortness of breath
- Extreme drowsiness, confusion, or slow or shallow breathing, especially if you also take a sleeping pill, anxiety medicine, or opioid
- Shakiness, sweating, and confusion that could be low blood sugar if you take diabetes medicine
- Repeated vomiting that keeps you from holding down fluids or your doses

**Call your doctor soon if you notice:**

- Severe or watery diarrhea, especially with fever or blood. This can be a sign of *C. difficile* infection, which can happen during or even weeks after antibiotics.
- Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or pain under the right ribs, which can signal liver problems (rare with clarithromycin, but described on the label)
- Muscle pain or weakness if you also take a statin

## Who Should Avoid Alcohol on Clarithromycin Entirely

Skip alcohol for the whole course, and ideally a few days after, if you:

- Are being treated for **H. pylori** or an ulcer
- Take **metronidazole or tinidazole** at the same time
- Take any **sedating medicine**: sleeping pills, benzodiazepines, opioids, or sedating antihistamines
- Have **heart disease**, a known long QT interval, or take other QT-prolonging drugs
- Have **diabetes** treated with insulin or sulfonylureas
- Have **liver or kidney disease**
- Are pregnant or breastfeeding (check with your doctor about the antibiotic and alcohol separately)

For a wider view of which medicines clash with alcohol, see our [alcohol and medications guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications).

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's popular as a hangover supplement. It's been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver, mostly in animal and lab research, with limited human data. It's not a treatment for infection and doesn't change anything about how you should take an antibiotic.

**While you're on clarithromycin, it's best to hold off on starting DHM or any new supplement.** Clarithromycin already affects how your body processes many substances, and some lab studies suggest DHM may affect certain drug-processing enzymes as well. There are no human studies of the two together. That's not proof of a problem, but there's no reason to add an unknown during a short course. Ask your pharmacist if you're already taking it.

Once your course is finished and you're back to normal social drinking, DHM is one option some people use alongside the basics: eating before you drink, pacing yourself, and alternating with water. There is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers outright, and it's no substitute for drinking less. If you want to try it, two well-reviewed options are [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) explains what to check with a pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

- Clarithromycin doesn't cause a disulfiram-like reaction, and the NHS says moderate drinking is allowed.
- The real risks come from **drug interactions** (it blocks CYP3A4, boosting many other medicines), **heart rhythm effects**, and **stomach side effects** that alcohol makes worse.
- **Avoid alcohol completely** during H. pylori treatment, especially if metronidazole is included, and for at least 72 hours after the last metronidazole dose.
- If you take sedatives, opioids, diabetes medicine, statins, or heart drugs, talk to your pharmacist before having any alcohol on clarithromycin.
- Never skip a dose because you've been drinking. Finishing the full course matters more than any single drink.

Erythromycin is clarithromycin's older relative and shares the same CYP3A4 problem, plus a stronger effect on how fast your stomach empties. Our [erythromycin and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/erythromycin-and-alcohol) covers it.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking clarithromycin?**

Clarithromycin does not cause the violent flushing-and-vomiting reaction that metronidazole and tinidazole can, and the UK's NHS guidance says drinking is allowed while you take it. Keeping it to a drink or two is the safer choice, though, because alcohol can worsen the antibiotic's stomach side effects, slow your recovery, and add to sedation from other medicines that clarithromycin makes stronger. If your prescription is part of an H. pylori kit that includes metronidazole, avoid alcohol completely. Check with your doctor or pharmacist about your own situation.

**Does alcohol make clarithromycin less effective?**

There is no good evidence that a moderate amount of alcohol stops clarithromycin from working. The bigger risks are indirect: heavy drinking can leave you dehydrated and run down, vomiting can bring up a dose before it is absorbed, and a big night makes it easier to forget a dose. Missed or vomited doses are a real reason a course can fail, so finish every dose on schedule.

**How long after clarithromycin can I drink alcohol?**

There is no official waiting period for clarithromycin itself, and most of the drug is cleared within about a day of the last dose. Its blocking effect on the liver enzyme CYP3A4 can last a few days longer, though, because the body has to build new enzyme. If you take other medicines that interact with clarithromycin, waiting two to three days is a reasonable cushion. If metronidazole was part of your treatment, wait at least 72 hours after the last metronidazole dose.

**Can I drink alcohol on H. pylori treatment with clarithromycin?**

Usually not. Many H. pylori regimens pair clarithromycin with metronidazole, and alcohol with metronidazole can cause flushing, pounding heart, nausea, and vomiting. Even in regimens without metronidazole, alcohol irritates an already inflamed stomach lining and can make ulcer pain and side effects worse. Most doctors advise skipping alcohol for the whole course, and with metronidazole for at least 72 hours after it ends.

**Is clarithromycin and alcohol bad for your heart?**

Clarithromycin can lengthen the QT interval, a part of the heart's electrical cycle, which in rare cases can trigger a dangerous rhythm. Binge drinking can lower potassium and magnesium through vomiting and fluid loss, and low levels of those raise that risk. A couple of drinks is very unlikely to matter for a healthy person, but people with heart disease, a known long QT, or who take other QT-prolonging drugs should talk to their doctor before drinking on clarithromycin.

**Is Biaxin the same as clarithromycin?**

Yes. Biaxin and Biaxin XL were brand names for clarithromycin, and most prescriptions today are filled with generic clarithromycin tablets, extended-release tablets, or liquid. The alcohol guidance is the same for all forms. The extended-release version is taken once a day with food, which can actually make it easier to plan a meal and keep the stomach settled.

**Can I take DHM while on clarithromycin?**

Ask your pharmacist first. Clarithromycin interacts with many drugs because it blocks a major liver enzyme, and some lab studies suggest DHM may affect drug-processing enzymes too. There are no human studies of the two together. The simplest choice is to wait until your antibiotic course is finished before starting any new supplement.
